nodes.description: Particle-induced fluid displacement or a proposed persistent mechanical load deflects the cupula outside its normal response to head acceleration.

evidence.snippet: The aberrant signal results when gravity pulls the particles through the endolymph canal creating a plunger‐like effect which in turn causes ipsidirectional cupular displacement

nodes.description: Cupular deflection bends vestibular hair-cell stereocilia and changes canal-afferent activity. In BPPV, the particle-driven component of that signal does not represent actual head rotation.

evidence.reference_title: Benign positional vertigo, its diagnosis, treatment and mimics.
evidence.snippet: Hair cells are directionally polarised therefore the direction of endolymph flow and subsequent deflection of the stereocilia, determines whether there is an excitatory or inhibitory response from the canal afferents.

evidence.reference_title: Benign positional vertigo, its diagnosis, treatment and mimics.
evidence.snippet: As the head moves with respect to gravity, the otoconia also move, activating semicircular canal afferents and producing a false sense of head rotation and nystagmus.

nodes.description: Reverse Epley or Yacovino head-hanging maneuvers are used for carefully diagnosed anterior-canal BPPV. Evidence is mainly from case series, and a central cause of downbeat nystagmus must be considered.

evidence.snippet: A review by Anagnostou and colleagues found mostly case series with the commonly used technique being the reverse Epley maneuver or the Yacovino maneuver.

nodes.description: Repositioning manoeuvre for the horizontal canal variant, rotating head and body in 90 degree increments through a full turn to walk geotropic canaliths back to the utricle. Used when the supine roll test shows geotropic horizontal nystagmus.

evidence.snippet: When horizontal geotropic nystagmus is encountered, a maneuver known as the barbecue roll or barrel roll can be used to reposition the canalith in the plane of the horizontal canal.

nodes.description: A particle mass becomes trapped at a canal narrowing or ampullary neck. Fixed obstruction can maintain abnormal cupular pressure and prolonged nystagmus. A mobile, reversible jam is a proposed cause of apogeotropic positional responses and treatment resistance that can resemble cupulolithiasis.

evidence.snippet: Canalith jam occurs when particles become entrapped at narrowings or bends in the canal or at the ampullary neck

These reversible jams result in a different clinical presentation than a fixed jam. The mobile plug can act as a check ball valve in the canal and cause an apogeotropic DCPN and vertigo symptoms identical to that usually ascribed to cupulolithiasis.

nodes.description: Canalith repositioning, usually an Epley or modified particle repositioning maneuver, is recommended for posterior canal BPPV. It moves canaliths toward the utricle. Repeat treatment may be needed, and successful treatment does not eliminate future recurrence. Mobility and cervical limitations affect maneuver selection.

evidence.snippet: More recently, a Cochrane review of 11 relevant studies representing 745 participants, concluded that the Epley maneuver and its modifications are safe and effective.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical Practice Guideline: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (Update).
evidence.snippet: treat, or refer to a clinician who can treat, patients with posterior canal BPPV with a canalith repositioning procedure

evidence.reference_title: Clinical Practice Guideline: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (Update).
evidence.snippet: The update group made a strong recommendation against postprocedural postural restrictions after canalith repositioning procedure for posterior canal BPPV.

nodes.description: Free particles move under gravity within a canal when head position changes. Their displacement produces a transient hydrodynamic stimulus. The usual delayed, crescendo-decrescendo response ends as particles settle; brief fatigue is compatible with particle dispersion.

evidence.snippet: The aberrant signal results when gravity pulls the particles through the endolymph canal creating a plunger‐like effect which in turn causes ipsidirectional cupular displacement

nodes.description: In this model, otoconial material adheres to the cupula and changes its effective density, producing gravity sensitivity and a relatively persistent positional response. Persistent adhesion in living patients has not been directly established; periampullary free particles and canalith jam can produce overlapping signs.

evidence.snippet: In the cupulolithiasis model, the particulate matter becomes adherent to the cupula itself. This cupular loading renders the system sensitive to gravitational forces
Evidence that otoconia adhere strongly or persistently to the cupula is lacking.

nodes.description: A canal-specific alternative to barbecue rolling for horizontal-canal BPPV. The maneuver variant and side depend on the positional nystagmus pattern; apogeotropic disease may require a conversion sequence before particle clearance.

evidence.snippet: A randomized control trial showed comparable success between Gufoni (response rate of 60.9%) and barbecue roll (69.1%).

nodes.description: Head trauma is a recognized antecedent of secondary BPPV and may mechanically dislodge otoconia. A meta-analysis found an association based on two trauma studies, with substantial heterogeneity; this does not exclude other routes to BPPV in younger people.

evidence.reference_title: Risk Factors for the Occurrence of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV): History, Pathophysiology, Office Treatment and Future Directions.
evidence.snippet: In younger individuals it is the commonest cause of vertigo following head injury.

nodes.description: A 2025 sham-controlled trial of 159 patients meeting clinical posterior-cupulolithiasis criteria found resolution of vertigo and nystagmus by the next day in 37.7% after head-shaking versus 13.2% after sham. Immediate efficacy was not significantly different, and mastoid oscillation did not significantly outperform sham. Long-term benefit was not measured. Clinical classification does not directly demonstrate particles adhering to the cupula.

evidence.reference_title: Treatment Maneuvers in Cupulolithiasis of the Posterior Canal Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
evidence.snippet: In the intention-to-treat analysis, 20 patients in the head-shaking group (37.7%), 14 in the mastoid oscillation group (26.4%), and 7 in the control group (13.2%) showed the resolution of vertigo and nystagmus the following day

evidence.reference_title: Treatment Maneuvers in Cupulolithiasis of the Posterior Canal Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
evidence.snippet: There were no significant differences in the therapeutic efficacy between the head shaking and mastoid oscillation groups (P = .21; α = .0167) or between the mastoid oscillation and sham groups (P = .09; α = .0167)

evidence.reference_title: Treatment Maneuvers in Cupulolithiasis of the Posterior Canal Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
evidence.snippet: we could not assess the long-term therapeutic efficacy of the head-shaking and mastoid oscillation maneuvers or the natural course of PC-BPPV-cu.

nodes.description: Abnormal semicircular-canal signaling is perceived as self-motion or environmental motion. Nausea and imbalance may accompany the vestibular disturbance; their presence and persistence vary.

evidence.snippet: In the case of BPPV, aberrant signals from semicircular canals create an illusion of motion which results in vertigo.

nodes.description: Nausea can accompany severe positional attacks and may also be provoked by diagnostic or therapeutic maneuvers.

evidence.snippet: can range in severity from mild dizziness to debilitating episodes that may induce nausea or vomiting

nodes.description: Displaced material reaches the canal lumen, most commonly the gravity-dependent posterior canal. Its nonampullary opening communicates with the utricle; the cupula partitions the canal-side ampulla from the utricular side. This anatomical route is distinct from particles approaching the utricular surface of a cupula.
nodes.id: Otoconial Debris Entry into a Semicircular Canal

evidence.snippet: With regular head movements, free‐floating endolymph debris can migrate into the posterior canal via its nonampullated end (common crus).

nodes.description: Age-related loss of otoconial mass and structural integrity is a proposed susceptibility process. These changes also occur outside BPPV; degeneration is not established as the initiating lesion in every patient.

evidence.reference_title: Age-Related Vestibular Loss: Current Understanding and Future Research Directions.
evidence.snippet: The otoconia contained in the utricle and saccule have also been shown to undergo morphological changes and degeneration during a human’s lifespan as observed in postmortem analyses

nodes.description: Brief recurrent vertigo triggered by changes in head position relative to gravity, such as lying back or rolling in bed. Canalithiasis attacks usually last less than a minute; persistent variants last longer. Some patients, especially older adults, describe nonspecific dizziness or falls rather than rotatory vertigo.

evidence.snippet: These vertigo spells usually last less than 20 seconds (longer for the horizontal canal) but may be accompanied by a lingering, nonspecific imbalance, so patients often overestimate the length of the attacks.

evidence.reference_title: Benign positional vertigo, its diagnosis, treatment and mimics.
evidence.snippet: Not all patients with BPV will report rotatory vertigo and may instead report dizziness, light-headedness or falls

nodes.description: Positionally elicited nystagmus with direction and timing dependent on the involved canal and mechanism. Typical posterior canalithiasis produces transient torsional upbeating nystagmus; persistent responses occur in other variants. Subjective BPPV describes compatible positional vertigo without observable nystagmus.

evidence.snippet: Characteristic nystagmus features include latency of onset, limited duration, torsional and upbeat directionality, reversibility, and fatigability.
During provocative maneuvers, some patients may experience vertigo without nystagmus. This is termed subjective BPPV

nodes.description: Canal occlusion is reserved for selected patients with intractable, disabling BPPV despite appropriate maneuvers. Plugging greatly reduces cupular responsiveness but can cause postoperative imbalance or hearing loss. Confirmation of the affected canal and assessment of hearing and vestibular function are important before surgery.

evidence.snippet: For a small subset of patients with intractable BPPV, canal occlusion can be considered.

evidence.reference_title: Benign positional vertigo, its diagnosis, treatment and mimics.
evidence.snippet: surgical occlusion of the canal may be warranted, although this carries a risk of permanent hearing loss and imbalance

nodes.description: Semont is an alternative repositioning maneuver for posterior canal BPPV. Its original rationale was liberation of adherent debris, but it also moves free canaliths; therapeutic benefit does not prove cupular adhesion. Rapid body movements may be difficult for patients with limited mobility.

evidence.snippet: Studies have found the Semont maneuver to be efficacious, safe, and advantageous compared to a sham‐control.

nodes.description: An extended Semont maneuver tested in posterior canalithiasis. In a per-protocol analysis of 195 of 214 randomized patients, an initial clinician treatment followed by nine home maneuvers daily shortened mean time to sustained symptom resolution to 2.0 versus 3.3 days with Epley. Single clinician-maneuver success did not differ significantly. Results concern this supervised-plus-home protocol, with patient-reported outcomes and uncertain home execution.

evidence.reference_title: The Semont-Plus Maneuver or the Epley Maneuver in Posterior Canal Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo: A Randomized Clinical Study.
evidence.snippet: For the secondary end point (effect of a single maneuver), no significant difference was detected (67 of 98 [68.4%] vs 61 of 97 [62.9%]; P = .42; α = .05).

evidence.reference_title: The Semont-Plus Maneuver or the Epley Maneuver in Posterior Canal Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo: A Randomized Clinical Study.
evidence.snippet: In this prospective randomized clinical trial, we found that in pcBPPV canalolithiasis, the SM-plus is more effective than the EM in terms of days until recovery

nodes.description: Dislodgement of otoconia, sometimes together with linking fibrils and otolithic membrane matrix, supplies mobile debris. The initiating cause is often unknown; aging-related change, trauma or another inner-ear disorder may contribute. Utricular origin is supported by the morphology of surgically recovered particles rather than direct observation of their detachment.

evidence.reference_title: Otoconia and otolithic membrane fragments within the posterior semicircular canal in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
evidence.snippet: The presence of whole otoconia within the particulate matter in our samples associated with attached and detached interconnecting fibrils suggests that fragments of the otolithic membrane with attached otoconia may become dislodged and displaced into the semicircular canal.

nodes.description: Abnormal canal input drives a compensatory slow eye movement and an oppositely directed fast phase through vestibulo-ocular pathways. The nystagmus axis helps identify the stimulated canal; posterior canalithiasis typically gives torsional upbeating nystagmus. Atypical patterns require consideration of peripheral variants and central mimics.

evidence.snippet: Activation of the ipsilateral inferior oblique and contralateral superior rectus during the Dix‐Hallpike leads to a torsional nystagmus (the top pole of the eye beats towards the lowermost ear) along with an up‐beating component.

nodes.description: Vomiting can accompany severe positional vertigo or be elicited during repositioning.

evidence.snippet: can range in severity from mild dizziness to debilitating episodes that may induce nausea or vomiting
